video_title: Lawfare Daily: The Houthi War Against Saudi Arabia
gist: With Iran blockading the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis have pushed south along Yemen's Red Sea coast toward the Bab el-Mandeb and are now explicitly targeting only Saudi oil tankers, threatening the East-West pipeline/Red Sea route that is Saudi Arabia's main Hormuz bypass. Former UN panel expert Greg Johnson argues that the Houthis are expansionist, increasingly independent of Iran, and aiming for Yemen's Marib-Shabwah-Hadramaut oil and gas fields. The anti-Houthi coalition and the Saudi-UAE partnership are too fractured to stop them, and neither airstrikes nor sanctions work, so the risk to Red Sea energy shipping should keep growing through 2027-28.

themes.theme: Hormuz + Bab el-Mandeb squeeze on Saudi oil

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia has three crude export routes: the Strait of Hormuz (cheapest), the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea coast and then south through the Bab el-Mandeb to Asia, or north through the Suez Canal and around Africa (very long and costly). With Iran closing Hormuz, the Houthis are trying to close the Bab el-Mandeb route as well.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: A simultaneous Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb disruption would leave only the costliest Saudi route open. That is bullish for crude and tanker rates and bearish for Saudi export volumes and Asian refiners that depend on Saudi barrels.
insights.quote: So Iran has closed down that eastern route. The Houthis say, "Hey, we can close down this southern route and put a lot of pressure on the Saudis."

insights.claim: In the current campaign, the Houthis say explicitly that they are targeting only Saudi oil tankers, not general commercial or Israel-linked shipping. The aim is to keep the United States out of the conflict after the costly US strikes of 2025.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Narrow targeting means risk premia fall mainly on Saudi-linked tankers and cargoes rather than all Red Sea transits. It also lowers the odds of a US military response that could reopen the route.
insights.quote: "We're only going after Saudi oil tankers."

insights.claim: By seizing Red Sea coastline near the Bab el-Mandeb, including the port of Mocha and some Red Sea islands, the Houthis can spread launchers along more coast so they are harder for the US to target. They can hit ships bunched up in the chokepoint and use cheaper 'dumb' weapons instead of longer-range ballistic missiles.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Cheaper attacks at the chokepoint make the threat to shipping more lasting and harder to deter. War-risk insurance and rerouting costs for Red Sea transits are likely to stay high.
insights.quote: I think it's a pretty significant shift.

insights.claim: The Houthi pressure on Saudi shipping is partly extortion. They want Riyadh to pay Yemeni civil servant salaries, and have at times demanded that Saudi Arabia pay the salaries of the Houthi fighters who are fighting it.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: A Saudi payoff deal could quickly de-escalate tanker risk. Headlines about Saudi-Houthi financial talks are a key signal for Red Sea risk premia.
insights.quote: they feel that Saudi Arabia's vulnerable and they're trying to squeeze

themes.theme: Houthi push for Yemen's oil & gas

insights.claim: Greg Johnson expects the Houthis to push east from Sana'a into Marib, then southeast into Shabwah (reaching the Gulf of Aden) and northeast into Hadramaut. That would take Yemen's 'triangle of power', the oil and gas fields that are the country's only real exports, and cut Aden off from Hadramaut.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Houthi control of Yemen's hydrocarbons would give them a lasting economic base. Watch fighting around Marib as a leading indicator of Houthi staying power and of wider Gulf of Aden shipping risk.
insights.quote: one analyst, and I think he's right on this, refers to this as sort of Yemen's triangle of power

insights.claim: The Houthis' territorial ambitions reach beyond Yemen to the Saudi border provinces of Asir and Najran, which were part of Yemen before 1934 and traditionally had a Zaidi Shia population.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Cross-border claims mean the risk to Saudi Arabia is territorial as well as maritime, which adds a lasting security discount to southern Saudi projects.

insights.claim: The Houthis treat every political agreement they sign as a way to buy time, rearm and regroup, so any ceasefire or deal with them should be expected to break down once they feel strong enough to take more territory.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Markets should fade relief rallies on Houthi ceasefire headlines. Previous deals have been temporary pauses, not resolutions.
insights.quote: the Houthis have basically looked at these agreements as something that they signed to buy time, which allows them to sort of refit and regroup

insights.claim: The Houthis have 'won' by simply surviving successive wars: six wars against the Yemeni government (2004-2010), the Saudi-led coalition air war (2015-2022), and about two months of heavy US airstrikes in 2025. Each survival has strengthened their belief that they hold a strong hand.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Air power alone has repeatedly failed to degrade the group. Military-escalation headlines should not be read as durable fixes for Red Sea shipping risk.
insights.quote: So, air power allow alone is not able to defeat them.

insights.claim: War benefits the Houthis domestically because their governance is heavy-handed and poor. In 2023-24 they used the popularity of the Palestinian cause in Yemen to attack shipping, invite strikes and recruit fighters, 'riding the wave' rather than starting it.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: The Houthis have a structural incentive to keep conflict going, so peace periods are fragile and new attacks should be expected whenever a regional crisis offers cover.
insights.quote: think of it like a surfer doesn't launch the wave, but the surfer rides the wave

insights.claim: Greg Johnson, a former member of the UN Security Council's Yemen Panel of Experts, sees the Houthis as aligned with Iran but not under its command and control. They depended heavily on Iranian medium-range ballistic missile components and IRGC advisers in 2017-18, which enabled strikes on Riyadh, Abu Dhabi and Dubai, but have since built their own defense industrial base.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: A US-Iran settlement or Iranian de-escalation would not necessarily stop Houthi attacks, because Red Sea risk is partly independent of Tehran.
insights.quote: the Houthis and Iran, their interests align rather closely, and it's a mutually beneficial relationship

insights.claim: The so-called internationally recognized government of Yemen is actually seven to ten rival factions, including Tariq Saleh's National Resistance Forces and the separatist Southern Transitional Council, who fight each other as much as the Houthis. That lets the unified Houthis avoid ever facing them all at once.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: There is no credible local ground force to roll back the Houthis, so Red Sea disruption risk looks structural rather than cyclical.
insights.quote: It's just that they never have to fight every other group put together.

insights.claim: In December 2025 Saudi Arabia bombed UAE shipments to the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council, which was trying to seize southern Yemen. Riyadh then pushed the UAE out of Yemen entirely, and the guest says the Saudi-UAE relationship there is too broken to salvage.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: An open Saudi-UAE rift weakens Gulf coordination on security and possibly OPEC+ cohesion, a geopolitical factor to watch for Gulf assets.
insights.quote: you actually had the very odd optics of Saudi Arabia bombing UAE shipments that were coming into Yemen to support the STC

insights.claim: Fully backing the anti-Houthi coalition as US ground proxies, as with the Kurds against ISIS, is not viable. Many southern groups have serious human-rights violations that US law restricts partnering with, success is doubtful, and neither the US, the UAE nor Saudi Arabia will commit ground troops.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: With no one willing to supply ground forces, the Houthi threat will keep growing, and markets should price persistent rather than transient Bab el-Mandeb risk.
insights.quote: nobody is really able to solve the Houthi problem, which means it just keeps metastasizing

insights.claim: US policy toward the Houthis has cycled through five options: defend-only naval escorts, strikes on mobile launchers (Operation Prosperity Guardian, early 2024), a big air campaign (Operation Rough Rider, 2025), going after Iran directly (Operation Midnight Hammer in 2025 and Operation Epic Fury in 2026), and backing local proxies. None has solved the problem.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: The options have been exhausted with no durable result, so geopolitical risk premia for Red Sea shipping and Gulf energy should be treated as persistent.

insights.claim: UN sanctions on Yemen backfired. The asset freezes hit former president Ali Abdullah Saleh, who had international assets, but not the Houthis, who had none. That weakened a Houthi rival, whom the Houthis then killed before absorbing his network.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Sanctions headlines targeting the Houthis should not be treated as de-escalation catalysts for shipping or energy risk.
insights.quote: all the sanctions actually did was weaken an internal Houthi adversary

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia has no good options against the Houthis. Doing nothing invites expansion, ground troops face unforgiving mountains, a decade of airstrikes has only made the Houthis stronger, and US strikes ended in a ceasefire. Riyadh is now asking China to lean on Iran to restrain the Houthis.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: China's role as a mediator, given its dependence on Gulf oil flows, is a key channel to watch for any easing of Red Sea tanker risk.
insights.quote: Saudi Arabia has reached out to China to try to put pressure on Iran to put pressure on the Houthis to get them to back down

insights.claim: Greg Johnson expects the Houthi problem to get steadily worse. Airstrikes are at best a holding action against a group with more strategic patience than Saudi Arabia or the US, and he expects today to look like 'the good old days' by 2027-28.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: The base case is rising, not falling, Red Sea and Gulf energy-transit risk over the next one to two years, which argues against pricing in normalization of Suez/Red Sea shipping.
insights.quote: the Houthis have strategic patience, which it seems Saudi Arabia and the US don't necessarily have

insights.claim: The Houthis are an example of a wider US national-security problem: groups with leverage over a waterway or natural resource that cannot be dislodged without an invasion the US will not undertake, and that airstrikes alone cannot subdue.
insights.speaker: Greg Johnson (guest, Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Chokepoint leverage by non-state actors is a recurring, underpriced risk across global shipping lanes and commodity supply chains.
